newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt dips but still locked in range-trade.
newsitem.headline: German debt dips but still locked in range-trade.

text.p: German debt slipped to losses in afternoon trading on Wednesday, still rivetted by any hints on the future of Europe's planned monetary union.
"Basically we were caught in range all day, but the market is still expected to be volatile with information on currency driving the trading," a dealer said.
By 1448 GMT the September Bund futures contract was trading down 10 basis points at 100.78 having hovered in a narrow range between 100.71 and 101.05 during the session.
The market was buffeted by strong resistance at 101 and support at 100.70, lacking the resistance to break away.

Dealers agreed the market remained fixated on any signals concerning Europe's currency union which is scheduled to begin in 1999 but has recently run into trouble as its two leading proponents, Germany and France, may not be ready to enter.
While the bond market was boosted by assurances made earlier this morning that there were no fundamental differences between France's president and prime minister.

This afternoon however the market became slightly more worried when German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the clock for Europe would not be stopped. Analysts said policy makers' insistence on a timely launch is in some ways worrying.

The Bundesbank council will meet on Thursday and discuss Bonn's asset revaluation plan, which is unlikely to affect the market however, dealers said. After the Bundesbank two weeks ago firmly rejected Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to receive a payout from the Bundesbank this year to help offset his gaping fiscal holes, the two sides appeared to be nearing a compromise.
As long as the Bundesbank sticks by its intentions to prevent any payout this year, the market is not expected to react, dealers said.

As Germany is currently struggling to meet the strict qualifications for EMU and France's new socialist government had expressed severe reservations about the project in general, economists worried the combination might lead to a watering down of criteria resulting in a weakened Euro.
"This is what the market is thinking and worrying about, and until all of this is cleared up things are going to remain pretty volatile here," another dealer added.
Even firmer U.S. Treasuries were not able to hoist German debt higher.
Dealers predicted more range trading for Thursday.
